```{r setup}
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
library(ggiraph)
library(maps)
library(sf)
library(patchwork)
library(htmltools)

df <- read.csv("HCDP_data/rainfall/new/day/statewide/partial/station_data/2026/03/rainfall_new_day_statewide_partial_station_data_2026_03.csv")

date_cols <- names(df)[grepl("X2026", names(df))]

df_long <- df %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = all_of(date_cols),
               names_to  = "date",
               values_to = "rainfall") %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(gsub("X", "", date), format = "%Y.%m.%d"))

df_stations <- df_long %>%
  group_by(Station.Name, Island) %>%
  summarise(total = sum(rainfall, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(total)) %>%
  head(10)

total_rain_in <- round(sum(df_long$rainfall, na.rm = TRUE) * 0.0394 /
                       length(unique(df_long$Station.Name)), 1)

daily_means <- df_long %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(mean_in = mean(rainfall, na.rm = TRUE) * 0.0394)
peak_day  <- daily_means$date[which.max(daily_means$mean_in)]

top_station <- df_stations$Station.Name[1]
top_island  <- df_stations$Island[1]
top_total   <- round(df_stations$total[1] * 0.0394, 1)
```

## Row {height="50%"}

### Column {width="60%"}

#### Daily Average Rainfall — Statewide

```{r}
df_daily <- df_long %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(mean_rainfall = mean(rainfall, na.rm = TRUE) * 0.0394)

p <- ggplot(df_daily,
            aes(x = date, y = mean_rainfall,
                text = paste0("Date: ", format(date, "%b %d"),
                              "<br>Rainfall: ", round(mean_rainfall, 2), " in"))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#7c3aed", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_line(colour = "#a78bfa", linewidth = 0.8, group = 1) +
  geom_point(colour = "white", size = 2) +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %d", date_breaks = "2 days") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Rainfall (in)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x      = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "#1a1a2e", colour = NA),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#1a1a2e", colour = NA),
        text             = element_text(colour = "white"),
        axis.text        = element_text(colour = "white"),
        panel.grid       = element_line(colour = "grey30"))

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") %>%
  layout(paper_bgcolor = "#1a1a2e",
         plot_bgcolor  = "#1a1a2e",
         font          = list(color = "white"))
```

### Column {width="40%"}

#### Big Island — Peak Day (`r format(peak_day, "%B %d")`) {.tabset}

##### 3D View

![](rayshader_output/kona_low_peak_v2.png)

##### Notes

**What this shows.** Daily rainfall draped over Big Island terrain. Bright yellow on the western (Kona / leeward) coast = where the heaviest rain fell.

**Why it matters.** Hawaii's normal rain is trade-wind driven: NE winds hit the eastern slopes and dump rain there, leaving the leeward Kona side dry. **Kona lows reverse this** — a low-pressure system pulls moisture in from the south and the leeward slopes take the brunt.

**Built with.** rayshader for 3D, AWS Terrain Tiles via elevatr for elevation, daily rainfall rasters from HCDP.

## Row {height="35%"}

#### Storm Progression — Big Island in 3D {.flow}

The four panels below show the same Big Island view across the kona low's lifecycle. Watch the rainfall (yellow/green) emerge on the leeward side, peak on March 13, then fade. Compare with the bar chart above — peaks line up.

```{r}
#| echo: false

panel <- function(label, img, peak = FALSE) {
  htmltools::div(
    htmltools::div(
      label,
      style = paste0(
        "color: ", if (peak) "#fbbf24" else "#a78bfa",
        "; text-align: center; font-weight: ", if (peak) "700" else "600",
        "; font-size: 0.95rem; margin-bottom: 0.4rem;"
      )
    ),
    htmltools::img(
      src   = img,
      style = "width: 100%; border-radius: 4px;"
    )
  )
}

htmltools::div(
  style = "display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr); gap: 1rem; padding: 0.5rem;",
  panel("March 10 — Calm before",          "rayshader_output/kona_low_day_10.png"),
  panel("March 13 — Peak (Kona side hit)", "rayshader_output/kona_low_day_13.png", peak = TRUE),
  panel("March 14 — Still wet",            "rayshader_output/kona_low_day_14.png"),
  panel("March 17 — Storm fading",         "rayshader_output/kona_low_day_17.png")
)
```

# Top Stations

## Row {height="100%"}

### Column {width="72%"}

#### Daily Heatmap + Station Map (Top 10)

```{r}
hawaii_map <- st_as_sf(map("world", region = "USA:Hawaii",
                           plot = FALSE, fill = TRUE)) %>%
  st_set_crs(4326)

df_heat <- df_long %>%
  filter(Station.Name %in% df_stations$Station.Name) %>%
  mutate(
    Station.Name = as.character(Station.Name),
    rainfall_in  = round(rainfall * 0.0394, 2),
    tooltip      = paste0("Station: ", Station.Name,
                          "\nDate: ", format(date, "%b %d"),
                          "\nRainfall: ", rainfall_in, " in"),
    data_id      = Station.Name
  )

df_map_points <- df %>%
  filter(Station.Name %in% df_stations$Station.Name) %>%
  mutate(
    Station.Name = as.character(Station.Name),
    total_in     = round(rowSums(select(., starts_with("X2026")), na.rm = TRUE) * 0.0394, 2),
    tooltip      = paste0("Station: ", Station.Name,
                          "\nIsland: ", Island,
                          "\nTotal: ", total_in, " in"),
    data_id      = Station.Name
  )

p_heat <- ggplot(df_heat,
                 aes(x = date,
                     y = reorder(Station.Name, rainfall, sum),
                     fill = rainfall_in,
                     tooltip = tooltip,
                     data_id = data_id)) +
  geom_tile_interactive(colour = "grey20") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "D", na.value = "grey30", name = "in") +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %d", date_breaks = "2 days") +
  labs(title = "Daily Rainfall — Top 10 Stations", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(axis.text.x       = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        plot.background   = element_rect(fill = "#1a1a2e", colour = NA),
        panel.background  = element_rect(fill = "#1a1a2e", colour = NA),
        text              = element_text(colour = "white"),
        axis.text         = element_text(colour = "white"),
        panel.grid        = element_line(colour = "grey10"),
        legend.background = element_rect(fill = "#1a1a2e"),
        plot.title        = element_text(colour = "white", face = "bold"))

p_map <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = hawaii_map, fill = "#2d4a6e", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point_interactive(
    data = df_map_points,
    aes(x = LON, y = LAT,
        colour  = total_in,
        tooltip = tooltip,
        data_id = data_id),
    size  = 6,
    alpha = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "D", name = "Total (in)") +
  labs(title = "Station Locations", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.background   = element_rect(fill = "#1a1a2e", colour = NA),
        panel.background  = element_rect(fill = "#1a1a2e", colour = NA),
        text              = element_text(colour = "white"),
        axis.text         = element_text(colour = "white"),
        panel.grid        = element_line(colour = "grey20"),
        legend.background = element_rect(fill = "#1a1a2e"),
        plot.title        = element_text(colour = "white", face = "bold"))

girafe(
  ggobj      = p_heat + p_map + plot_layout(widths = c(1.6, 1)),
  width_svg  = 16,
  height_svg = 9,
  options = list(
    opts_sizing(rescale = TRUE, width = 1),
    opts_hover(css     = "fill:orange; stroke:white; stroke-width:1.5;"),
    opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.25;"),
    opts_selection(type = "single",
                   css  = "fill:orange; stroke:white; stroke-width:2;"),
    opts_toolbar(saveaspng = TRUE)
  )
)
```

### Column {width="28%"}

#### About this view

**Linked highlighting.** Hover over a row in the heatmap and the matching station glows on the map. Click a dot on the map and the corresponding heatmap row pulses.

**What you're seeing.** The heatmap (left) shows daily rainfall in inches for the 10 stations that received the most total rain in March 2026. Stations are ordered top-to-bottom by total monthly rainfall — the wettest is at the top.

**Reading the kona low.** The bright vertical band running down most stations around **March 12–14** is the kona low's fingerprint. Most Hawaii rainstorms are localized — they hit only certain windward stations. A statewide event where almost every top station lights up at once is unusual.

**Geography.** Most top-10 stations sit on the windward (NE) side of their island where rain normally falls. But for this event, leeward stations also took heavy hits — another kona low signature, since these systems pull moisture in from the south and dump it on slopes that are usually shielded.
